title: Scrambled character detective
instruction: Each scrambled text appeared because the browser read the bytes in a different encoding from the one the website was saved in. Match it with the original word. Clue: in UTF-8, every Czech letter with a háček or an accent has two bytes, and Windows-1250 reads every byte as one character.

pairs.why: The letter č is the byte pair C4 8D in UTF-8. Windows-1250 reads C4 as Ä and 8D as Ť. The letters a and j have the same byte in both encodings, so they survived.
ž = C5 BE. In Windows-1250, C5 is the character Ĺ and BE is the character ľ. Two bytes become two characters.
ř = C5 99, and the byte 99 in Windows-1250 is the ™ sign. That’s why a scrambled ř looks like a trademark.
š = C5 A1, and A1 is the háček ˇ on its own. Notice: ř, ž, š and ů all start with the same byte C5, so they all start with the character Ĺ.
ý = C3 BD (Ă˝) and ě = C4 9B (Ä›). Suddenly four letters become six characters.
ů = C5 AF, and AF in Windows-1250 is the letter Ż.

pairs.b: čaj uložený ve Windows-1250, čtený jako UTF-8
pairs.why: The opposite direction. Windows-1250 saves č as a single byte E8. For UTF-8, E8 is the start of a group of three bytes, but right after it comes an ordinary a. That sequence of bytes isn’t valid in UTF-8, so the browser shows the replacement character �.

debrief: Scrambled characters aren’t random: each pattern reveals where the encodings didn’t match. Ä and Ĺ at the start of little groups mean: saved in UTF-8, read as Windows-1250. A question mark in a diamond means the opposite. The cure is one line in the page’s head, <meta charset="utf-8">, and a file saved in UTF-8.
